Why Wichita Homes Need Pest Control

Wichita's climate is deceptively challenging for homeowners. With an average high of 69°F and an average low of 50°F, the temperature range creates constant movement in pest populations. When you factor in 33 inches of annual rainfall and 10 inches of snowfall, you're looking at consistent moisture that attracts everything from termites to ants to cockroaches.

The city's housing stock tells part of the story. With 1,233 total housing units serving a population that's grown significantly over generations, many homes have aging foundations and entry points that become highways for pests during seasonal changes. Neighborhoods near Delano, around Lincoln Park, and through Oak Park all experience similar issues—older homes with character, but also with vulnerabilities.

Kansas has faced 100 federal disaster declarations in the last decade, with 99 of those being severe storms. That kind of weather pattern doesn't just damage property—it displaces pest populations and drives them into structures. The National Weather Service ICT office monitors Sedgwick County closely using KICT radar because weather here shifts fast. Those same storms that bring heavy rain also bring pest pressure that lingers long after the skies clear.

The Arkansas River runs through Wichita with a current stream discharge of 451 cubic feet per second and a gauge height of 3.56 feet, maintaining normal flow that supports thriving insect populations year-round. While most of Wichita falls into FEMA Flood Zone X—minimal flood risk outside the 500-year floodplain—the moderate flood risk areas still see enough moisture intrusion to create ideal conditions for moisture-loving pests.
